prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A 13-year-old Minnesota boy who has cancer has resumed chemotherapy treatments and is not responding well, a family spokesman said Friday. Doctors say Daniel Hauser's lymphoma responded well to a first round of chemotherapy in February. Danny Hauser started a second round of chemotherapy treatment this week, Jim Navarro said in a statement on the family's Web site, dannyhauser.com. "The doctor changed the number of chemotherapy drugs in the protocol submitted to the court. Danny is not tolerating the drugs well and has been vomiting all day. He is understandably angry and depressed about being forced to go through the ravages of chemotherapy again." Daniel underwent his first round of chemotherapy in February, a month after he was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. But his parents were concerned about the treatment's side effects, which typically include nausea, and decided to end the chemotherapy regimen and pursue holistic treatments instead. When Daniel's oncologist learned of the decision to reject standard treatment, which doctors say is associated with a cure rate of as high as 90 percent, he asked a court to intervene to ensure the teen got chemotherapy. Doctors say that, without it, the disease would likely prove fatal. But last week, before the court could act, Colleen Hauser packed up her son and flew with him to Southern California, from where they were planning to continue to Mexico to seek alternative alternative medical treatment. She said he would have run on his own had she not helped him flee. She changed her mind before crossing the border and returned this week with Daniel to Minnesota, where the family agreed to comply with whatever treatment the court ordered. A medical examination revealed that the boy's tumor had grown since he was diagnosed and the boy's doctor recommended he resume chemotherapy. After examining the boy on Monday, Dr. Michael Richards estimated the tumor's size at 5.3 inches by 5.1 inches by 6.3 inches, and said it was "protruding outside the chest wall." He said initiation this week of standard chemotherapy treatment was "imperative." Richards recommended at least another five cycles of chemotherapy followed by radiation, and added that the "goal will be to include alternative therapies in which the family is interested, as long as there is not data to suggest that a particular danger exists with any alternative medicine." District Court Judge John Rodenberg originally took custody of the boy away from his parents, but returned him to his family on the condition that they comply with the recommendations of the cancer specialist. Hodgkin's lymphoma is a cancer that affects the lymphatic system, which is part of the immune system. As the disease progresses, it compromises a body's ability to fight infection. CNN's Aaron Cooper contributed to this story.

**Minnesota teen resumes court-ordered chemotherapy after return from Mexico**

**MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota** — A 13-year-old cancer patient who briefly fled Minnesota with his mother to pursue alternative treatment in Mexico has resumed court-ordered chemotherapy, according to the family’s attorney.

Daniel Hauser, who was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma, returned to Minnesota with his mother, Colleen Hauser, after a nationwide search. The two disappeared after a judge ruled that Daniel needed conventional medical treatment and ordered his parents to cooperate with doctors.

Daniel had undergone one chemotherapy session but stopped after experiencing severe side effects. His family sought alternative therapies based in part on their religious beliefs, prompting authorities to argue that refusing further chemotherapy amounted to medical neglect.

Doctors have said Daniel’s cancer is highly treatable with chemotherapy and radiation, with a strong chance of recovery. Without established treatment, they warned, the disease could be fatal.

After returning from Mexico, Daniel was evaluated at a Minneapolis hospital and began another round of chemotherapy. His parents agreed to follow a treatment plan developed with his doctors while remaining under court supervision.

The case drew national attention and raised difficult questions about parental rights, religious freedom and the government’s responsibility to protect a child facing a life-threatening illness.

counterfactuals.output:
**Court Orders Treatment in Daniel Hauser Cancer Dispute**

**NEW ULM, Minn. —** The case of Daniel Hauser, a 13-year-old Minnesota boy with Hodgkin lymphoma, became a national test of parental rights, religious freedom and the state’s authority to require potentially lifesaving medical care.

Daniel was diagnosed in January 2009 with Hodgkin lymphoma, a cancer of the lymphatic system. His pediatric oncologist, Dr. Bruce Bostrom of Children’s Hospitals and Clinics of Minnesota, testified that Daniel had roughly a **90 to 95 percent chance of being cured** if he completed the recommended treatment. Without conventional therapy, Bostrom said, Daniel’s chance of survival was approximately **5 percent**.

Daniel received one chemotherapy treatment in February but declined further sessions. His family said the treatment made him severely ill and conflicted with their preference for natural medicine. Daniel and his mother, Colleen Hauser, identified with the Nemenhah, a religious organization that promotes Native American-inspired spiritual practices and alternative healing.

Doctors said the initial chemotherapy had reduced Daniel’s chest tumor, but that it subsequently began growing again. Medical testimony indicated that the mass had increased from about **2.5 centimeters to approximately 4.5 centimeters** after treatment stopped, demonstrating that the disease remained active.

Bostrom recommended that Daniel complete a standard course consisting of **six rounds of chemotherapy followed by radiation treatment**. The doctor said the combined regimen offered a very high likelihood of cure, while delay risked allowing the lymphoma to spread and become more difficult to treat.

Daniel’s parents argued that forcing chemotherapy would violate their rights and Daniel’s wishes. The state countered that a minor could not refuse care when the proposed treatment was well established, had a strong probability of success and was necessary to prevent death.

Brown County District Judge John Rodenberg found that Daniel’s parents had **medically neglected** him by withholding recommended treatment. The judge concluded that Daniel did not fully understand the nature of his illness or the consequences of refusing therapy. He ordered a new medical evaluation and directed that treatment proceed if doctors continued to recommend chemotherapy.

The court placed Daniel in the **temporary legal custody of Brown County for purposes of obtaining medical care**, while initially allowing him to remain physically with his parents under court supervision. When Daniel and his mother failed to appear for a scheduled examination and left Minnesota, the judge issued an arrest warrant for Colleen Hauser and ordered authorities to locate the boy. They later returned voluntarily.

The custody order did not permanently terminate the parents’ rights. Rather, it gave county officials authority over Daniel’s cancer treatment so that chemotherapy and radiation could be administered despite the family’s objections. Daniel ultimately resumed conventional treatment after his return.
